title: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
summary: Run a whole cluster's real code in one deterministic process with simulated network, disk and time, inject aggressive faults, check invariants, and replay any failure exactly from its seed.
outcomes: Explain why timing-dependent distributed bugs are hard to reproduce and how a seeded simulation makes a run a pure function of code and seed
Trace a discrete-event simulator loop and compute how often a seeded network reorders messages
Compute BUGGIFY firing probabilities and explain why swarm testing beats one tuned configuration
Design safety and liveness oracles, such as the cycle test and a healed-quorum liveness phase
Judge when DST fits a system, what it cannot catch, and how to replay and confirm a fix

lessons.title: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce

blocks.md: From the consensus course you know that Raft and Paxos are only correct if they survive crashes, lost messages, reordered messages and slow nodes. The protocol on paper may be proven safe, but the code that implements it is not. Its bugs typically need a specific *combination* of events: a message delayed past a timeout, a crash right after a write, a partition that heals at an awkward moment.

Those combinations are driven by **nondeterminism**: inputs to the program that are not fixed by the test itself. In a real cluster the main sources are:

- **Scheduling**: which thread or task runs next.
- **Network**: when each message arrives, in what order, and whether it arrives at all.
- **Time**: what the clock reads when a timeout is checked.
- **Randomness**: random numbers seeded from the operating system.
- **Disk**: how long each write takes and what survives a power loss.

Because each run sees different values for all of these, a failure you saw once may never come back. Suppose a bug fires in a fraction $p$ of runs. The chance of seeing it at least once in $n$ independent runs is $1-(1-p)^n$, and the chance of seeing it *again* when you try to debug it is exactly the same, no better.

blocks.title: Chance of hitting a rare bug at least once

scenes.caption: With $p$ = 0.001 you need about 2,994 runs to have a 95% chance of seeing the bug once (computed as ln 0.05 / ln(1 - p)).
At $p$ = 0.0001 it takes about 29,956 runs. And after you see it once, reproducing it under a debugger costs the same number of runs all over again.
Rarer bugs push the curve right. Drag the slider: every factor of 10 in rarity costs a factor of 10 in runs, for finding and again for reproducing.

blocks.prompt: Your CI saw a test fail once in 30,000 runs with an unreadable log. You put the test in a loop overnight to catch it again with full tracing. If the real rate is 1 in 10,000, how many runs do you need for a 95% chance of one more failure?
blocks.reveal: About **29,956** runs, the same as before. Past runs give you no head start, because each run draws fresh timing from the machine. This is why distributed bugs get closed as "cannot reproduce". Deterministic simulation changes the cost of reproducing from tens of thousands of runs to **one** run: re-run the same seed.

blocks.md: Classic approaches each give up something. Unit tests are reproducible but walk one path and inject no faults. Fault injection on a real cluster (the approach of Jepsen) runs the real code under partitions and crashes, but the FoundationDB paper notes that all such approaches *lack deterministic reproducibility*. Model checking explores exhaustively, but it verifies a model of the protocol rather than the implementation you ship.

**Deterministic simulation testing** (DST) combines the strengths. You run the *real* code of every node, all inside one process (FoundationDB uses a single thread), and route every source of nondeterminism through interfaces that a simulator implements. The simulator draws every random choice (latency, drops, crashes, which task runs next) from one pseudo-random number generator started from a **seed**. Same code plus same seed gives exactly the same run.

blocks.title: Same node code, two worlds behind the interfaces

scenes.caption: The node code talks to the world through four interfaces. In production each one is a thin shim over the real system call.
In simulation the same code runs unchanged, but each interface is a fake: a simulated network, disk, clock and random source.
Every fake draws its choices from one seeded generator. Seed 42 always yields the same latencies, drops, crashes and clock readings, so the whole run is a pure function of (code, seed).

blocks.md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

blocks.question: Jepsen-style fault injection and DST both inject partitions and crashes into real code. What does DST add that changes day-to-day debugging most?
options: It tests a formal model instead of the code, so it is exhaustive
Any failing run can be replayed exactly from its seed
It needs no changes to how the system does I/O
It runs on real hardware, so timing is realistic
blocks.explain: Determinism is the key addition: a failure becomes a seed you can replay, step through and add logging to. DST does test the real code (not a model), it usually *does* require routing I/O through simulated interfaces, and its timing is simulated, not real.

blocks.question: A team wants maximal certainty that their *protocol design* has no safety bug for 3 nodes and up to 2 crashes, before writing any code. Which tool fits that goal best?
options: Deterministic simulation testing of the implementation
Running the cluster in production with extra logging
Model checking a specification of the protocol
blocks.explain: Before code exists there is nothing to simulate. Model checking can exhaustively explore a small specification. The FoundationDB paper's tradeoff: model checking can be more exhaustive, but it checks a model; DST checks the real implementation and is reproducible. Many teams use both.

lessons.title: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time

blocks.md: At its core a deterministic simulator is a **discrete-event simulation**. There is a queue of future events, each stamped with a simulated time. The main loop repeatedly pops the earliest event, sets the simulated clock to its time, and runs its handler. Handlers may schedule more events (a message sent now is delivered at now plus a latency). Nothing ever sleeps: the clock jumps straight to the next event.

Here is a complete toy simulator in Python. Node A sends two messages to node B, *set x = 1* at time 0 and *set x = 2* at time 1. The network delays each message by a latency between 1 and 10 ms, drawn from a generator seeded with the run's seed. B keeps whatever value arrived last. The invariant is that B ends with 2, the value A sent last.

blocks.code:
import heapq, random

class Sim:
    def __init__(self, seed):
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)   # the ONLY randomness
        self.now = 0                     # simulated ms
        self.queue, self.seq = [], 0

    def at(self, t, event):
        heapq.heappush(self.queue, (t, self.seq, event))
        self.seq += 1                    # breaks ties deterministically

    def run(self):
        x = 0                            # node B's register
        while self.queue:
            t, _, (kind, val) = heapq.heappop(self.queue)
            self.now = t                 # jump, never sleep
            if kind == "send":           # A sends "set x = val"
                latency = self.rng.randint(1, 10)
                self.at(self.now + latency, ("deliver", val))
            else:                        # B applies the last message seen
                x = val
        return x

sim = Sim(seed=5)
sim.at(0, ("send", 1))
sim.at(1, ("send", 2))
assert sim.run() == 2, "B ended with a stale value"
blocks.caption: A whole simulator in about 25 lines. The event tuple is (time, sequence, event); the sequence number makes equal times deterministic.

blocks.title: Running seed 5 step by step
blocks.code:
import heapq, random

class Sim:
    def __init__(self, seed):
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)   # the ONLY randomness
        self.now = 0                     # simulated ms
        self.queue, self.seq = [], 0

    def at(self, t, event):
        heapq.heappush(self.queue, (t, self.seq, event))
        self.seq += 1                    # breaks ties deterministically

    def run(self):
        x = 0                            # node B's register
        while self.queue:
            t, _, (kind, val) = heapq.heappop(self.queue)
            self.now = t                 # jump, never sleep
            if kind == "send":           # A sends "set x = val"
                latency = self.rng.randint(1, 10)
                self.at(self.now + latency, ("deliver", val))
            else:                        # B applies the last message seen
                x = val
        return x

sim = Sim(seed=5)
sim.at(0, ("send", 1))
sim.at(1, ("send", 2))
assert sim.run() == 2, "B ended with a stale value"

scenes.caption: Before running, the queue holds the two send events. The clock is at 0 and B's register is 0.
Pop (0, send 1). The generator for seed 5 draws latency 10, so delivery of 1 is scheduled at time 10.
Pop (1, send 2). The next draw is latency 5, so delivery of 2 lands at time 6, before the delivery of 1.
The clock jumps from 1 to 6 with no waiting. B applies set x = 2.
The clock jumps to 10 and the stale set x = 1 overwrites it. The run returns 1 and the assertion fails. Running seed 5 again reproduces this exactly.
scenes.output: AssertionError: B ended with a stale value

scenes.caption: Seed 4: latencies 4 and 5. Message 1 lands at 4, message 2 at 6, so B ends with 2. Pass.
Seed 5: latencies 10 and 5. Message 2 overtakes message 1, so B ends with the stale 1. Fail.
Seed 7: latencies 6 and 3. Message 2 lands at 4, message 1 at 6. Fail again, through a different schedule.

blocks.prompt: Latencies are independent and uniform on 1 to 10 ms, and ties go to the event scheduled first. What fraction of seeds should fail?
blocks.reveal: Message 1 is delivered at $l_1$ and message 2 at $1+l_2$. B is stale when $l_1 > 1 + l_2$, i.e. $l_1 - l_2 \geq 2$. Counting the 100 equally likely pairs gives $8+7+\dots+1 = 36$, so **36%**. Running the script over seeds 0 to 999 found 346 failing seeds, close to that. A tie ($l_1 = 1 + l_2$) passes because message 1 got the smaller sequence number, so the outcome is still fixed by the seed.

blocks.md: **Simulated time is cheap time.** Wall-clock cost depends only on how many events are processed, not on how much simulated time passes. A 1.5 second election timeout with nothing else happening costs one event. The FoundationDB paper makes this point: discrete-event simulation can run arbitrarily faster than real time when CPU utilization in the simulation is low, because the simulator fast-forwards the clock to the next event.

blocks.title: Speedup over real time, from a simple cost model

scenes.caption: Model (simplified): speedup = 1 / (events per simulated second x CPU seconds per event). Three nodes heart-beating every 100 ms give 30 events/s; at 20 us each, 10 simulated minutes (18,000 events) take 0.36 s, about 1,667x.
A busy simulation at 100,000 events per simulated second runs at 0.5x: slower than real time. Speed comes from idle stretches, not magic.

Cheaper events shift the line up (the two marked points assume 20 us per event). Real reports vary: TigerBeetle describes its VOPR as running at about 1000x speed; FoundationDB's docs report about 10x more simulated time than wall time.

blocks.md: Determinism leaks are easy to write. Reading the real clock, spawning an OS thread, seeding from OS entropy, or iterating a hash map whose order is randomized per process (Rust's default `HashMap` is) all make the same seed produce different runs. FoundationDB avoids multithreaded concurrency entirely and deploys one node per core instead.

blocks.question: A replica computes its election deadline as `time.time() + random_timeout()`, using Python's real clock, while everything else goes through the simulator. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the timeout value still comes from the seeded generator
Replay: the deadline now depends on wall-clock time, so the same seed can schedule different events
Only performance: real clock reads are slower than simulated ones
Safety of the protocol in production
blocks.explain: Wall-clock time differs between runs and is unrelated to simulated time, so the deadline, and every event that depends on it, changes from run to run. One leak like this destroys reproducibility for the whole simulation. All time must come from the simulated clock.

blocks.question: Why does the toy simulator put a sequence number between the time and the event in each queue entry?
options: So events at the same simulated time pop in a fixed order on every run
To make the heap faster
To count how many messages were lost
So that later events can be cancelled
blocks.explain: Two events can share a timestamp. Without a deterministic tie-breaker their order would depend on incidental details (here, Python would even try to compare the event payloads). The sequence number makes the order a function of the order of scheduling, which is itself determined by the seed.

lessons.title: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing

blocks.md: A deterministic simulator with polite defaults would be a slow, reproducible version of a normal test. Its power comes from being **hostile**. The FoundationDB simulator injects machine, rack and datacenter failures and reboots, network faults, partitions and latency, and disk misbehavior such as corrupting unsynchronized writes when a machine reboots. It also randomizes event times. TigerBeetle's VOPR drops and reorders packets, partitions the network, and corrupts reads and writes to its simulated disk.

Hostile does not mean maximal. The FoundationDB paper warns that fault distributions are tuned to avoid driving the system into a *small* state space through an excessive fault rate. If every node crashes every second, the cluster never gets far enough to reach the interesting states, such as a leader change (a *view change* in Viewstamped Replication terms) during a long recovery.

FoundationDB engineers once held an informal competition for the most effective fault pattern. The winner is **swizzle-clogging**: pick a random subset of nodes, *clog* (stop) their network connections one by one over a few seconds, then unclog them one by one in a random order. The docs say this pattern is particularly good at finding deep issues.

scenes.caption: Healthy cluster. The simulator picks a random subset to swizzle: here n2, n3 and n5.
Clog n2 first. Its connections stop delivering, but the others keep running and react to a slow peer.
A moment later clog n3, then n5. The cluster now passes through a sequence of partial partitions, not one clean split.
Unclog in a random order, n5 first. n5 rejoins with stale state while n2 and n3 are still silent.
Then n2, then n3. Each step creates a new combination of who can hear whom, which is where recovery and leader-change code tends to break.

blocks.md: Network and disk faults come from outside the code. FoundationDB also lets the code **cooperate** in its own torture through *buggification*. At many places the code asks the simulator for permission to do something unusual but still within its contract: return an error from an operation that usually succeeds, add a delay to something usually fast, or pick an odd value for a tuning parameter. Randomizing tuning parameters also ensures a particular tuning value never silently becomes necessary for correctness.

blocks.caption: The two probabilities are the defaults in FoundationDB's Buggify.h. Production builds never take the branch.

blocks.prompt: A buggified site is evaluated 10 times during a run. In what fraction of runs does it fire at least once? Why might FoundationDB want most runs to never fire it?
blocks.reveal: $P = 0.25 \times (1 - 0.75^{10}) \approx 0.236$. In 75% of runs the site is inactive and in another 1.4% it is active but never fires, so about **76%** of runs take the normal path there. That is deliberate: if every site fired constantly, every run would look the same (always slow, always erroring) and some behaviors would never happen. Randomly switching sites on and off per run produces many *different* mixtures.

blocks.title: P(a buggified site fires at least once in a run)

x.label: evaluations of the site per run k

scenes.caption: With FoundationDB's defaults (0.25 and 0.25), one evaluation fires with probability 0.0625, ten with 0.236.
However often the site is reached, the curve saturates at 0.25: in three runs out of four this site is simply switched off for the whole run.
Raising the per-evaluation probability only makes the curve climb faster. The activation probability sets how many runs see this behavior at all.

blocks.md: This idea has a name: **swarm testing** (Groce et al., ISSTA 2012). Instead of one tuned random-test configuration that enables every feature, you run a *swarm* of configurations that each omit features at random. Their example: a stack with a capacity bug that crashes above 32 items. A generator that mixes pushes and pops evenly almost never gets that deep, because pops keep the stack shallow. FoundationDB applies the same idea: each run gets a random cluster size, workloads, fault parameters, tuning parameters, and a random subset of enabled buggify sites.

blocks.title: Stack overflow bug: one config vs a swarm (64-op tests)

scenes.caption: Computed exactly by dynamic programming for 64-operation tests (simplified: the paper uses varying lengths). The default config overflows past 32 items in only 0.004% of tests.
The swarm gives each test one of {push only, pop only, both} with equal chance. Push-only tests always overflow, so 33.3% of all tests hit the bug, about 8,300x more often.

blocks.md: To find rare bugs, maximize the *diversity* of runs, not the intensity of each one. Random per-run choices of faults, features and buggify sites cover far more distinct states than one heavily tuned configuration.

blocks.question: Using FoundationDB's defaults, what is the probability that two specific buggify sites are *both* activated in the same run?
blocks.explain: Each site is activated independently with probability 0.25 once per run, so both are active with $0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.0625$, about 1 run in 16. Rare pairs still happen often across tens of thousands of runs per night.

blocks.question: A teammate sets the network drop rate to 50% in every simulation run to "find more bugs". What is the likely effect?
options: More bugs found, since more faults always means more coverage
The cluster rarely makes progress, so the run explores a small, repetitive set of states
Determinism breaks, because drops are random
Nothing, because consensus tolerates any drop rate
blocks.explain: The FoundationDB paper explicitly tunes fault distributions to avoid an excessive fault rate that drives the system into a small state space. At 50% loss on every run the cluster mostly retries and times out; deep states such as long recoveries under load are rarely reached. Vary the rate per run instead.

lessons.title: Knowing a run went wrong: invariants, oracles and liveness

blocks.md:
A simulator only finds the bugs it can *detect*. The check that decides whether a run is correct is called a **test oracle**. Real DST systems layer several kinds:

- **Assertions in the code**. TigerBeetle has thousands of assertions and keeps them on in production, on the theory that stopping is better than continuing in an incorrect state.
- **Workload invariants**, properties of the data that only hold if transactions behave correctly.
- **Cross-checks**, for example TigerBeetle's checkers that caught-up replicas have byte-for-byte identical data files.
- **Recovery checks**, which ask whether the system comes back once the environment heals.

FoundationDB's **cycle test** is a beautiful workload invariant. It stores $N$ keys that form a ring: key $n$ holds the pointer $(n+1) \bmod N$. Each transaction picks a random key $r$, reads $r_2 = \text{next}(r)$, $r_3 = \text{next}(r_2)$, $r_4 = \text{next}(r_3)$, then writes $r \to r_3$, $r_2 \to r_4$, $r_3 \to r_2$. That swaps two neighbors and keeps a single ring. The check walks the pointers from key 0 and expects to visit all $N$ keys before returning.

scenes.caption: Start: key n points to n+1, and key 4 points back to 0. Walking from 0 visits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: one ring of length 5.
Transaction A picks r = 1 and reads keys 1, 2, 3: r2 = 2, r3 = 3, r4 = 4.
A writes 1 to 3, 2 to 4, 3 to 2. Keys 2 and 3 swap places in the ring. The walk is 0, 1, 3, 2, 4: still all 5 keys.
Transaction B picked r = 2 but read the ring *before* A committed: r2 = 3, r3 = 4, r4 = 0. If isolation is broken and B commits anyway, it writes 2 to 4, 3 to 0, 4 to 3.
Result: 0 to 1 to 3 to 0. The walk closes after 3 keys and keys 2 and 4 are orphaned. The check fails, exposing the isolation bug no matter which component caused it.
Correct behavior: the database aborts B (it read keys A wrote) and B retries on the new ring. Then it writes 2 to 0, 4 to 1, 0 to 4, and the walk is 0, 4, 1, 3, 2: intact.

blocks.md: Good invariants are cheap to check and impossible to satisfy by accident. The cycle test does not care *how* isolation broke (a proxy bug, a lost conflict check, a bad recovery). Any lost or interleaved write corrupts the ring.

Invariants like these check **safety**: nothing bad ever happens. **Liveness** means something good eventually happens, for example the cluster keeps committing whenever a majority is healthy. Liveness is harder to test, because uniformly random faults eventually *heal*. TigerBeetle found that its VOPR, which crashed, restarted and partitioned replicas uniformly at random, could not catch liveness bugs that a later fault would accidentally fix.

Their fix was a second phase they call **liveness mode**. After a period of normal random faults, the simulator:

1. picks a quorum of replicas to be the healthy *core*,
2. restarts any core replica that is down,
3. heals all partitions between core replicas,
4. makes every fault involving non-core replicas **permanent**.

Then it runs for a while and requires the core to process all transactions. FoundationDB's paper describes the same shape: return the environment to a state where recovery should be possible, then verify the cluster eventually recovers.

blocks.title: A liveness bug found by TigerBeetle's liveness mode

scenes.caption: Setup from the TigerBeetle post: A is missing ops 5 and 6. B has op 6 but not 5; C has op 5 but not 6. Together B and C hold everything A needs.
A repairs both ops in parallel and spreads requests round-robin with a counter. Request 1 goes to B for op 5, request 2 goes to C for op 6. Both lack what was asked.
Next round: the counter has advanced by 2, so it is back in phase. Op 5 goes to B again and op 6 to C again, the worst possible pairing.

This repeats forever. In safety mode a random restart of A reset the counter and hid the bug; in liveness mode nothing heals it, so the simulator reports a replica still missing entries after a timeout.

blocks.md: How do you know the simulator actually reaches a scenario you care about? FoundationDB uses **conditional coverage macros**: a developer worried about the full-buffer case adds `TEST( buffer.is_full() );`, and the simulation results report how many distinct runs hit that condition. If the count is zero or tiny, they add buggification, workloads or faults until it is not.

blocks.question: Your DST suite injects only crashes that always restart within 2 simulated seconds and partitions that always heal within 5. Which bug is it most likely to miss?
options: Two leaders committing different values in the same term
A follower that never catches up while one peer stays permanently down
A torn write corrupting the log
An off-by-one in log index comparison
blocks.explain: That is a liveness bug, and it hides whenever faults heal on their own, exactly as in TigerBeetle's resonance bug. The other options are safety violations that can show up under transient faults. To catch liveness bugs, make some faults permanent and require a healthy quorum to keep making progress.

blocks.question: Why is the cycle test's check (walk from key 0, expect N distinct keys) a stronger oracle than checking that each transaction returned success?
options: It runs faster than checking return codes
It never needs to read the database
It catches lost or interleaved writes even when every transaction reported success
It tests liveness instead of safety
blocks.explain: Isolation bugs typically return success while corrupting data. The ring property can only survive if every committed transaction behaved as if it ran alone, so it detects silent corruption that per-call results cannot. It is still a safety check.

lessons.title: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it

blocks.md: When a simulation fails, the output is tiny: a seed and the code version. TigerBeetle's docs say the seed plus the Git commit is enough to replay the exact simulation and bug locally. From there debugging is ordinary single-process debugging: set breakpoints, add logging, re-run as often as you like.

Adding logs is safe because, as the FoundationDB paper notes, extra logging generally does not affect the deterministic order of events. A log line does not consume random numbers or schedule events. The paper adds that when a bug was first found in production, the team's first step was usually to improve the simulation until it reproduced the bug there, and only then to debug it.

blocks.title: From a nightly failure to a fix

scenes.caption: The swarm runs many seeds in parallel. Randomized testing is embarrassingly parallel, so FoundationDB developers burst extra capacity before major releases.
A failing run reports only its seed and commit. Replaying them reproduces the failure exactly, every time.
Iterate: add logging, re-run, inspect. Logging does not change event order, so the bug cannot vanish while you watch it.
After the fix, the specific scenario becomes a targeted test, and the random swarm keeps exploring new seeds against the new code.

blocks.prompt: You fix the bug, re-run the failing seed, and it passes. Does that prove the fix works?
blocks.reveal: Not by itself. The seed replays exactly only on the **same code**. Your fix may change how many random numbers are drawn or which events are scheduled, so the same seed can now drive a completely different execution that never reaches the old scenario. This is why TigerBeetle pairs the seed with the commit. Confirm a fix by reasoning about the replayed trace, by a targeted test that forces the scenario (TigerBeetle keeps such specific cases in its `replica_test.zig`), and by many new seeds.

blocks.title: What each testing approach gives you

scenes.caption: Simplified summary, building on the FoundationDB paper's related-work discussion (1 = yes). Real-cluster fault injection runs real code under faults but lacks deterministic reproducibility.
Model checking can be more exhaustive than simulation, but it verifies a model rather than the actual implementation.
DST gives real code, faults and reproducibility together. It is still a random search: it can never prove the absence of bugs, only make finding them cheap.

blocks.md:
The FoundationDB paper is frank about limits:

- Simulation cannot reliably detect **performance** problems, such as an imperfect load-balancing algorithm.
- It cannot test **third-party libraries** or any code not written against the simulated interfaces. FoundationDB therefore avoided external dependencies; it replaced Apache ZooKeeper with its own Paxos after real-world fault injection found two bugs in ZooKeeper.
- Bugs in the **filesystem or OS**, or a misunderstanding of their contract, still bite. Several FoundationDB bugs came from the real OS contract being weaker than the team believed: the simulation can only be as harsh as the team's understanding of the real contract.

A passing simulation is only as good as its fault model and its oracles. If your simulated disk never loses unsynced writes, you have not tested crash recovery; if no oracle checks liveness, a stuck cluster passes.

There are two ways to get determinism, as the Antithesis docs put it. **Design it in**: write the system so every nondeterministic component is pluggable. FoundationDB built its Flow runtime for this, TigerBeetle stubs out clock, network and disk for its VOPR, and Rust libraries such as turmoil and MadSim provide simulated runtimes, networks and filesystems. This is generally impractical for systems already in production. **Or impose it from outside**: run ordinary software inside a deterministic hypervisor, which is Antithesis's approach.

The payoff is documented. FoundationDB's docs report tens of thousands of simulations every night and an estimated equivalent of about one trillion CPU-hours of simulation overall; the paper credits simulation for letting a small team attempt ground-up rewrites of major subsystems. TigerBeetle runs its simulator 24/7 on 1024 cores against the latest version.

DST turns rare, timing-dependent bugs into seeds. The engineering cost is up front (every source of nondeterminism behind an interface, plus good oracles), and the return is that every bug found is a bug you can replay and fix.

blocks.question: Which system is the *weakest* fit for designing DST in from the start?
options: A new replicated log written in-house with its own network and disk layer
A large existing service built on many third-party clients, thread pools and direct system calls
A consensus library whose I/O already goes through small traits
A storage engine with a single-threaded event loop
blocks.explain: Designing DST in requires every source of nondeterminism to be pluggable, which is hard to retrofit across many dependencies and threads. The Antithesis docs call it generally impractical for systems already in production; that is the case a deterministic hypervisor targets. The other three are close to the FoundationDB and TigerBeetle shape.

blocks.question: Your simulation suite has been green for months, yet production suffers a throughput collapse under a skewed workload. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The simulator is not deterministic
The seeds were reused
Simulation does not reliably detect performance issues such as poor load balancing
The cycle test has a bug
blocks.explain: The FoundationDB paper lists this exact limitation: simulated time and simulated hardware do not model real performance well enough to catch problems like imperfect load balancing. Performance needs separate testing on real hardware, which FoundationDB does nightly in an environment called Circus.
